analysis.one_liner: Requires the EPA to set a legal national drinking-water limit for perfluorinated chemicals within two years.
analysis.headline: The bill to force a national drinking-water standard for perfluorinated compounds never left committee: it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in September 2016 and got no further action before the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have amended the Safe Drinking Water Act to require the EPA, within two years, to publish a health goal and issue a national regulation setting a legal limit for perfluorinated compounds (PFCs) in public drinking water. PFCs are manufactured chemicals used in many consumer products that accumulate in human blood. Today there is no enforceable national limit for these chemicals in drinking water, so communities with contamination have no federal standard to rely on. The bill was sponsored by a Democrat from Pennsylvania and cosponsored by two Republicans, both also from Pennsylvania, where contaminated water near military bases has been a documented problem.
analysis.who_benefits: The tens of millions of Americans whose public water systems are contaminated, or potentially contaminated, with perfluorinated compounds. An enforceable national limit would require utilities to test for these chemicals, tell customers when levels exceed the standard, and install treatment where needed. Residents near industrial sites and military installations where firefighting foams were used would gain a federal backstop instead of depending on state-by-state action.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the EPA, within two years of enactment, to publish a maximum contaminant level goal and issue a national primary drinking water regulation for perfluorinated compounds, the two steps that create an enforceable legal limit on a chemical in tap water.
Overrides any other deadline in the Safe Drinking Water Act to make the PFC regulation mandatory rather than discretionary, taking the timing out of the agency's own hands.

analysis.who_pays: Public water utilities that would have to test for the chemicals and install treatment systems, and pass those costs to ratepayers, plus the manufacturers and industrial and military users of the chemicals, who would face a federal legal standard for the first time and greater exposure to liability and cleanup expectations.

drawbacks.text: The two-year deadline is aggressive. Water utilities, and even some public-health officials, have argued in similar rulemakings that the testing, engineering, and cost estimates needed for a defensible limit for an entire class of chemicals can take longer, and a rushed standard risks being overturned in court.

Treating perfluorinated compounds as one class is broader than regulating the two most-studied ones individually; that can force utilities to control many chemicals at once, raising compliance costs that fall partly on households through water bills.
A federal limit also creates a compliance cost for water systems of every size, and small rural systems with few ratepayers face the steepest per-household treatment costs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a federally enforceable cap on a class of chemicals that accumulates in human blood and is not otherwise limited in drinking water — the core function the Safe Drinking Water Act exists to perform. The costs are real: treatment, testing, and higher water bills, borne partly by households and partly by utilities and the chemical industry. The bill's main weakness is its speed, not its purpose; a longer deadline would have reduced the risk of a flawed or overturned rule while still producing a standard. On balance, the public health benefit of a legal limit outweighs the compliance costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on September 22, 2016 — the last weeks before an election — sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Brendan Boyle introduced the bill on September 22, 2016, joined by two Pennsylvania Republicans, Patrick Meehan and Brian Fitzpatrick.

The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day it was introduced, and no further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the record before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.
The bill required the EPA to publish a maximum contaminant level goal and promulgate a national primary drinking water regulation for perfluorinated compounds within two years of enactment.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers and users of perfluorinated compounds, and the water utilities that avoided new testing and treatment requirements, were better off because the bill died: no federal legal limit for these chemicals in drinking water was created by this bill, and the EPA faced no binding deadline.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Chemical makers and their industrial users

for.name: Rep. Brendan F. Boyle
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to force an EPA drinking-water regulation for perfluorinated compounds.

for.name: Reps. Patrick Meehan and Brian Fitzpatrick
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, joining the Pennsylvania delegation push for a federal limit on PFCs in drinking water.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and took no further action; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor; with the committee taking no action, there was nothing to schedule, and the bill died when the 114th Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan from the start — a Democrat joined by two Republicans, all three from Pennsylvania — and it was never voted on, so no party split can be measured; its failure reflects committee inaction rather than a recorded opposition vote.

industries.industry: Perfluorinated compound manufacturers and industrial/military users (e.g. firefighting foam)
industries.note: A national drinking-water regulation would have created the first enforceable federal limit on these chemicals, exposing their past and ongoing use to regulatory and liability pressure. The bill's death left that pressure off.

The bill would have required utilities to test for PFCs and treat contaminated water, passing costs to ratepayers; but a clear federal standard also gives utilities a defined target instead of a patchwork of state rules and litigation risk.
